title: Blood Groups & Compatibility Testing
summary: The immunology of blood groups and the lab steps that make transfusion safe.

lessons.title: The ABO System: Antigens, Antibodies & Genetics

levels.kid:
Your red blood cells wear tiny name tags made of sugar. Some cells wear an **A** tag, some wear a **B** tag, some wear both, and some wear none. That is your **blood type**: A, B, AB or O.

Your body also has guards in the blood called **antibodies**. The guards attack any tag your own cells do not have. If you are type A, your guards attack B tags.

That is why doctors must match blood carefully. If the wrong blood goes in, the guards clump the new cells together and break them. That can make a person very sick.

You get your blood type from your parents. Mom gives you one instruction and Dad gives you one. Together they decide your tags.
levels.hs:
The **ABO system** is the most important blood group system for transfusion. It was discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1901, work that earned him a Nobel Prize.

**Antigens** are molecules that the immune system can recognize. ABO antigens are short sugar chains on the surface of red cells (and many other cells):
- Type A has A antigen
- Type B has B antigen
- Type AB has both
- Type O has neither, only the base structure called **H antigen**

What makes ABO special is that people naturally carry **antibodies** (anti-A and/or anti-B) against the antigens they lack, even if they have never been transfused. A type A person has anti-B; type O has both anti-A and anti-B; type AB has neither.

If type A blood is given to a type O patient, the patient's anti-A binds the donor cells, activates **complement** (a set of immune proteins) and bursts them inside the blood vessels. This **acute hemolytic transfusion reaction** can cause fever, low blood pressure, kidney failure and death.

Genetics: the **ABO gene** on chromosome 9 has three main versions (**alleles**): A, B and O. A and B are **codominant**, and O is recessive. So genotype AO gives type A, AB gives type AB, and OO gives type O.

Type O red cells are called the **universal donor** red cells. AB patients are **universal recipients** of red cells.
levels.college:
**Building the antigens.** ABO antigens are carbohydrate epitopes made by enzymes called **glycosyltransferases**, which add sugars one at a time:
- The **FUT1** gene encodes a fucosyltransferase that adds fucose to a precursor chain, creating **H antigen**.
- The **ABO gene** (chromosome 9q34) encodes a transferase that modifies H. The A enzyme adds **N-acetylgalactosamine**; the B enzyme adds **galactose**.
- The common O allele carries a single-base deletion (c.261delG) that shifts the reading frame, so it produces no working enzyme. H is left unmodified, which is why group O cells carry the most H.

The A and B enzymes differ by only four amino acids, yet these changes switch which sugar is added.

**Natural antibodies.** Anti-A and anti-B appear within the first months of life, likely triggered by similar carbohydrate structures on gut bacteria and food. Because the body does not make antibodies to its own antigens, each person makes antibodies only against the antigens they lack. These **isohemagglutinins** are mostly **IgM**, which agglutinates red cells at room temperature and fixes complement efficiently. That is why ABO mismatch causes brisk intravascular hemolysis.

**Frequencies** vary by population. In people of European ancestry, roughly 45% are O, 40% A, 11% B and 4% AB. Group B is more common in parts of Asia.

**Compatibility rules:**
- Red cells: the donor cells must lack antigens the recipient has antibodies against. O cells suit all recipients.
- Plasma: the logic reverses, because plasma carries the antibodies. **AB plasma** is the universal plasma.

**Blood typing** uses two checks. **Forward typing** tests the patient's cells with reagent anti-A and anti-B. **Reverse typing** tests the patient's plasma against known A1 and B cells. The two results must agree; a discrepancy has to be resolved before group-specific blood is issued.
levels.phd:
**Subgroups and structural heterogeneity.** The A antigen is not uniform. **A1** and **A2** account for most group A people. The A2 transferase (often from a single-base deletion near the 3' end that lengthens the protein) converts H less efficiently, leaving fewer A sites per cell: roughly 1 million on A1 cells versus about 250,000 on A2 cells. About 1-8% of A2 and 22-35% of A2B individuals make **anti-A1**, usually clinically insignificant cold IgM. The lectin from *Dolichos biflorus* identifies A1 cells. Weaker subgroups (A3, Ax, Ael) and B variants can cause forward/reverse discrepancies. **Cis-AB** alleles encode a single enzyme able to add both sugars, which can confuse family studies.

**Precursor chains and secretor status.** H can be built on type 1 or type 2 precursor chains. On red cells it sits mainly on type 2 chains. Secretions are governed by **FUT2** (secretor locus). About 80% of people are **secretors** with soluble ABH in saliva. Nonsecretor FUT2 status protects against some norovirus strains, an elegant host-pathogen link.

**The Bombay phenotype** (Oh), first described in Mumbai in 1952, results from homozygous null FUT1 and FUT2. These individuals lack H, so even a functional A or B enzyme has nothing to modify. They make potent anti-H and can receive only Bombay blood. Their cells type as O in standard testing, but anti-H lectin (*Ulex europaeus*) reveals the absence of H.

**Evolutionary and disease associations.** ABO polymorphism has been maintained by balancing selection for millions of years and is shared with other primates. Group O carries about 25-30% lower plasma **von Willebrand factor** and factor VIII levels, partly because A and B glycans on VWF slow its clearance. This translates into lower venous thromboembolism risk. Group O has also been linked to a higher risk of peptic ulcer and some protection against severe *Plasmodium falciparum* malaria, through reduced rosetting. Genome-wide studies have confirmed the ABO locus among risk loci for pancreatic cancer and thrombosis. The early COVID-19 association signals proved modest and inconsistent.
levels.expert:
**Why ABO errors still kill.** Most fatal ABO-incompatible transfusions come from **clerical and identification errors**, not serologic failure: a mislabeled sample ("wrong blood in tube") or bedside misidentification. Hemovigilance programs such as the UK's SHOT scheme track these errors. Two practices address them. First, many centers require **two separately drawn samples** to confirm the group before issuing group-specific red cells. Second, electronic bedside barcode checks verify patient identity at the point of transfusion. Because a group O recipient has potent anti-A and anti-B, an error involving an O patient is the most dangerous.

**Typing pitfalls clinicians should recognize:**
- **Neonates** make essentially no isohemagglutinins in the first months of life, so reverse typing is omitted. Any anti-A or anti-B detected is usually maternal IgG.
- **Weak or absent antibodies** in elderly patients and in hypogammaglobulinemia produce missing reverse reactions.
- **Acquired B**: bacterial deacetylases (for example in colorectal cancer or sepsis) convert A-antigen GalNAc to a B-like galactosamine, so a group A patient falsely types AB.
- **Leukemia** and other hematologic malignancies can weaken antigen expression.
- **Mixed-field** reactions follow massive transfusion of O cells or a bone marrow transplant.

**Transplantation.** ABO antigens are expressed on endothelium, so ABO matters for solid organs. ABO-incompatible kidney transplants are now routine with antibody removal (plasmapheresis or immunoadsorption) and B-cell depletion with rituximab. Infant hearts can cross ABO barriers before isohemagglutinins mature (West et al., 2001). In hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, ABO is not a barrier to engraftment. However, major mismatch causes delayed red cell engraftment and **pure red cell aplasia**, while minor mismatch causes **passenger lymphocyte** hemolysis about 1-2 weeks after transplant.

**Plasma and platelets.** Group O platelets and plasma carry high-titer anti-A/B that can hemolyze recipient cells. Many centers therefore titer donors or use group A plasma as an emergency universal plasma, an approach with good safety data in trauma.

**Frontiers.** Enzymes from gut bacteria (*Flavonifractor plautii*, Rahfeld et al., 2019) efficiently strip A antigen to create universal-donor-like cells. Converting donor kidneys and lungs ex vivo with these enzymes is in early study. Open questions include residual immunogenicity and durability in the body.

keyPoints: ABO antigens are sugar chains built on H antigen by glycosyltransferases
A adds N-acetylgalactosamine; B adds galactose; O makes no working enzyme
People naturally make IgM anti-A/anti-B against antigens they lack
ABO mismatch causes complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis
A and B are codominant; O is recessive (ABO gene, chromosome 9)
O red cells are universal donor cells; AB plasma is universal plasma

test.q: Chemically, ABO antigens on red cells are mainly:
test.explain: ABO antigens are sugar epitopes added by glycosyltransferases, not the proteins themselves.

test.q: Which antibodies does a group O person normally have in plasma?
test.explain: Group O cells lack A and B antigens, so the plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B.

test.q: The A transferase adds which sugar to H antigen?
test.explain: The A enzyme adds N-acetylgalactosamine; the B enzyme adds galactose. N-acetylglucosamine is a similar-sounding sugar but is not what the A enzyme adds.

test.q: Why does ABO mismatch cause rapid hemolysis inside blood vessels?
test.explain: Anti-A and anti-B are mainly IgM, which activates complement efficiently and bursts red cells.

test.q: A parent with genotype AO and a parent with BO could have a child of type:
choices: Any of A, B, AB or O
Type O, but not type AB
Type A or type B, not AB
Type AB, but not type O
test.explain: Each parent can pass either allele, so AB, AO, BO and OO are all possible: types AB, A, B and O.

test.q: Which red cells can be given to patients of any ABO group?
test.explain: O cells lack A and B antigens, so recipient anti-A/anti-B have nothing to bind.

test.q: Universal donor plasma comes from which blood group?
test.explain: AB plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B. O plasma contains both antibodies.

test.q: Testing a patient's plasma against known A1 and B cells is called:
test.explain: Reverse typing detects the plasma's antibodies; forward typing tests the cells' antigens.

test.q: Why does the common O allele make no working enzyme?
test.explain: A single-base deletion (c.261delG) shifts the reading frame, so the protein is not functional.

test.q: The base structure that A and B enzymes modify is called ___ antigen.
test.explain: FUT1 makes H antigen, which the A and B transferases then modify.

test.q: Who discovered the ABO blood groups in 1901?
test.explain: Karl Landsteiner's discovery made safe transfusion possible and won a Nobel Prize.

test.q: Because A and B alleles are both expressed together, they are called ___.
test.explain: In an AB person both enzymes work, so both antigens appear on the cells.

kidTest.q: What are blood type tags made of?
kidTest.explain: The A and B tags are made of sugar.

kidTest.q: A type A person's guards attack which tag?
kidTest.explain: Guards attack tags your own cells do not have.

kidTest.q: Which blood type has no A or B tags?
kidTest.explain: Type O cells wear neither tag.

kidTest.q: Where do you get your blood type from?
kidTest.explain: Each parent gives you one instruction for your blood type.

kidTest.q: What does wrong blood do to the new cells? It makes them c _ _ _ _ together.
kidTest.explain: The guards stick the wrong cells together and break them.

advancedTest.q: A patient types as O with standard reagents but has potent antibody against group O cells. The most likely explanation is:
choices: Acquired B from a bacterial deacetylase
advancedTest.explain: Bombay individuals lack H, so they type as O but make anti-H, which reacts with O cells rich in H.

advancedTest.q: Why does group O carry lower venous thrombosis risk?
choices: O cells adhere less to the endothelium
Faster clearance lowers VWF and factor VIII
advancedTest.explain: VWF lacking A/B glycans is cleared faster, lowering VWF and its carried factor VIII by about a quarter.

advancedTest.q: A group A patient with colorectal cancer and sepsis suddenly types AB with a normal reverse type. Best explanation:
choices: Bacterial enzymes form a B-like antigen
Transfused O cells give a mixed field
A cis-AB allele was newly inherited
advancedTest.explain: Acquired B arises when bacterial deacetylases convert A GalNAc to a B-like sugar. Plasma still has anti-B, so the forward and reverse types disagree.

advancedTest.q: Two weeks after a minor ABO-mismatched stem cell transplant (O donor, A recipient), hemolysis appears. The mechanism is:
choices: Pure red cell aplasia from host antibody
Delayed engraftment of donor red cells
Donor B cells making anti-A against host cells
advancedTest.explain: Passenger lymphocytes from the O donor make anti-A against the recipient's A cells. Pure red cell aplasia instead follows major mismatch.

lessons.title: The Rh System & Hemolytic Disease of the Fetus and Newborn

levels.kid:
Your red blood cells wear tiny name tags on the outside. One important tag is called **D**. If your cells have it, you are **Rh positive**. If they don't, you are **Rh negative**. Most people are positive.

Here is the tricky part. If a mom is Rh negative and her baby is Rh positive, a little of the baby's blood can sneak into the mom's blood, usually at birth. Her body thinks the D tag is a stranger and makes defenders called **antibodies**.

In a later pregnancy, those defenders can cross over and attack the next baby's red cells. That can make the baby sick and yellow.

The good news: doctors give the mom a special shot that stops her body from ever learning to fight D.
levels.hs:
Besides ABO, the most important blood group for transfusion and pregnancy is the **Rh system**. Its key antigen is **D**, a protein on the red cell membrane. People with D are **Rh positive** (about 85% of people of European ancestry, and higher in African and East Asian populations). People without it are **Rh negative**.

Unlike ABO, Rh-negative people don't naturally carry anti-D antibodies. They make anti-D only after exposure to D-positive red cells, through transfusion or pregnancy. This process is called **alloimmunization** (making antibodies against another person's antigens).

This matters in **hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN)**:
- An Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby (D inherited from the father).
- Fetal cells enter her blood, mostly at delivery, and she makes anti-D.
- Her anti-D is **IgG**, which crosses the placenta. In the next D-positive pregnancy it destroys fetal red cells (**hemolysis**).
- The baby can become anemic, swollen with fluid (**hydrops fetalis**), and jaundiced from **bilirubin**, a breakdown product of hemoglobin.

The first pregnancy is usually spared because sensitization happens late, and the first antibody response is weak.

Prevention is one of medicine's great successes. **Rh immune globulin** (anti-D, brand names like RhoGAM) is given to Rh-negative mothers during pregnancy and after delivering a D-positive baby. It clears fetal cells before her immune system responds.
levels.college:
**Genetics and structure.** The Rh antigens are carried on two homologous proteins encoded by adjacent genes on chromosome 1: **RHD** (D antigen) and **RHCE** (C/c and E/e antigens). The proteins are multipass membrane proteins associated with the **RhAG** glycoprotein. Most D-negative Europeans are homozygous for a complete **RHD deletion**. In people of African ancestry, the inactive **RHD pseudogene (RHDΨ)** is a common cause of D negativity. There is no "d" antigen; lowercase d just means D is absent.

**Immunogenicity.** D is the most immunogenic red cell antigen after A and B. Historically, a large share of D-negative recipients of a D-positive unit formed anti-D (estimates range roughly from 20% to 80%, depending on the study). Hence D type is matched routinely and D-negative women of childbearing potential receive D-negative blood.

**Pathophysiology of HDFN.**
- **Fetomaternal hemorrhage** sensitizes the mother: at delivery, or with miscarriage, abortion, ectopic pregnancy, amniocentesis, abdominal trauma, or external cephalic version.
- Primary response: IgM first, then IgG. Secondary response in a later pregnancy: rapid, high-titer IgG.
- IgG crosses the placenta via the **neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)**. Coated fetal cells are destroyed mainly by macrophages in the fetal spleen (**extravascular hemolysis**).
- Consequences: fetal anemia, **extramedullary hematopoiesis** (enlarged liver and spleen), erythroblasts in blood (hence the old name *erythroblastosis fetalis*), high-output heart failure and **hydrops**.
- In utero, the placenta clears bilirubin. After birth, the immature liver can't keep up, so unconjugated bilirubin rises. This risks **kernicterus**, bilirubin damage to the basal ganglia.

**ABO protection.** If mother and fetus are ABO incompatible (for example, an O mother with an A baby), maternal anti-A clears fetal cells quickly and lowers the risk of anti-D formation.

**ABO HDFN** itself is common but usually mild. Fetal A/B antigens are weakly developed, and A/B substances in tissues soak up the antibody.
levels.phd:
**Rh protein biology.** RhD and RhCE (each ~417 amino acids, 12 transmembrane passes) form a complex with RhAG, an ammonia/CO2 channel homologue. The complex links to the cytoskeleton via ankyrin and protein 4.2. D differs from RhCE at ~35 amino acids. Its epitopes are conformational and distributed across extracellular loops. **Rh-null** phenotype (RHAG mutations, regulator type; or RHCE plus RHD loss, amorph type) causes stomatocytosis and compensated hemolysis, showing that the complex is structurally important.

**D variants.** Missense changes in RHD produce:
- **Weak D**: reduced antigen density from transmembrane/intracellular substitutions. Types 1, 2 and 3 rarely make alloanti-D.
- **Partial D** (e.g., DVI, DIIIa, DAR): altered or missing epitopes, often from RHD-RHCE hybrid genes. Carriers can make anti-D against the missing epitopes. DVI is the classic clinically significant category.
- **DEL**: very low expression detectable only by adsorption-elution. It is common in East Asians (RHD*DEL1, c.1227G>A).

**Antibody effector biology.** Anti-D is predominantly IgG1 and IgG3. It does not fix complement efficiently because D sites are sparse (~10,000–30,000 per cell) and too widely spaced for C1q bridging. Destruction is therefore FcγR-mediated (FcγRIIIa, FcγRI) in the spleen. Severity correlates with IgG subclass, Fc glycosylation (afucosylated IgG1 binds FcγRIIIa more strongly), and titer.

**How anti-D prophylaxis works remains debated.** Proposed mechanisms include rapid clearance of antigen before presentation, epitope masking, and FcγRIIB-mediated inhibition of B-cell activation. Antibody-mediated immune suppression (AMIS) occurs even when clearance is incomplete and can operate against epitopes not targeted by the antibody, so simple clearance doesn't fully explain it.

**History.** Levine and Stetson (1939) described a transfusion reaction in a mother who had delivered a stillborn infant. Landsteiner and Wiener (1940) described the rhesus-related antibody. It was later shown that the rabbit anti-rhesus reagent recognized LW, not D, but the name stuck. The Liverpool (Clarke, Finn, Sheppard) and New York (Freda, Gorman, Pollack) groups introduced anti-D prophylaxis in the 1960s. It cut Rh HDFN deaths dramatically.
levels.expert:
**Antenatal management.** Every pregnant patient gets ABO/D typing and an antibody screen early in pregnancy. A D-negative, unsensitized patient receives routine antenatal Rh immune globulin around 28 weeks (some programs give two injections) and again postpartum if the newborn is D-positive. Additional prophylaxis follows sensitizing events. A **Kleihauer–Betke** test or flow cytometry for fetal hemoglobin quantifies large fetomaternal hemorrhage so coverage can be adjusted. A pitfall: passive anti-D shows up on the antibody screen for weeks. A titer that stays low, with a documented injection, points to passive antibody, but true sensitization must be excluded.

**Cell-free fetal DNA.** Noninvasive testing of maternal plasma for fetal RHD now lets many countries (Denmark, Netherlands, UK and others; increasingly the US) give targeted prophylaxis only to mothers carrying D-positive fetuses. This avoids exposing about 40% of D-negative women to an unnecessary plasma product. Pitfalls include the RHDΨ pseudogene and maternal weak/partial D alleles causing false results, and low fetal fraction early in pregnancy.

**The alloimmunized pregnancy.** Serial maternal titers are followed until a laboratory-specific critical titer is reached (commonly 16–32 for anti-D). Monitoring then switches to **middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity** Doppler. A value above 1.5 multiples of the median predicts moderate to severe fetal anemia, because anemic blood is less viscous and flows faster. This replaced serial amniocentesis (Liley curves). Treatment is **intrauterine transfusion** of O D-negative, irradiated, CMV-safe, fresh, high-hematocrit red cells into the umbilical vein. **Anti-Kell** is the classic exception to titer-based rules. It suppresses fetal erythropoiesis as well as causing hemolysis, so anemia appears at low titers.

**Recent advances.** **Nipocalimab**, an FcRn-blocking antibody, lowers maternal IgG and reduces placental transfer. In the phase 2 UNITY trial it delayed or avoided intrauterine transfusion in severe early-onset HDFN, and phase 3 (AZALEA) is under way. IVIG and plasmapheresis are older bridging options.

**Neonatal care.** Management uses phototherapy, IVIG for rising bilirubin, and **exchange transfusion** for severe hyperbilirubinemia. Late anemia from ongoing hemolysis can persist for weeks.

**Open problems.** Rh immune globulin is still made from hyperimmunized donors. The donor pool is shrinking, and no monoclonal replacement has matched polyclonal efficacy in trials. This supports interest in recombinant or engineered alternatives.

keyPoints: Rh positive means red cells carry the D antigen, encoded by RHD on chromosome 1
Rh-negative people make anti-D only after exposure through transfusion or pregnancy
Maternal IgG anti-D crosses the placenta via FcRn and destroys fetal red cells (HDFN)
HDFN causes fetal anemia, hydrops and, after birth, dangerous unconjugated bilirubin
Rh immune globulin given antenatally and postpartum prevents sensitization
MCA Doppler, intrauterine transfusion and cell-free fetal RHD testing guide modern care

test.q: A person is called Rh positive when their red cells carry which antigen?
test.explain: Rh positive means the D antigen is present. A and H belong to the ABO system, and Kell is a separate minor blood group.

test.q: How does anti-D usually arise in an Rh-negative person?
choices: It is inherited from the mother
test.explain: Unlike anti-A and anti-B, anti-D is not naturally occurring. It forms after transfusion or pregnancy exposure to D-positive cells.

test.q: Which antibody class crosses the placenta and causes HDFN?
test.explain: IgG is moved across the placenta by FcRn. IgM is too large to cross.

test.q: Why is a first Rh-incompatible pregnancy usually spared?
choices: The placenta breaks down maternal anti-D
Fetal cells lack D until after birth
Fathers pass D mainly to later children
test.explain: Most fetomaternal hemorrhage occurs at delivery, so maternal antibodies form too late to harm the first baby but threaten later ones.

test.q: What is the main danger of high unconjugated bilirubin in a newborn with HDFN?
test.explain: Unconjugated bilirubin can deposit in the basal ganglia and cause kernicterus, a form of brain damage.

test.q: How does ABO incompatibility between mother and fetus affect anti-D formation?
test.explain: Maternal anti-A or anti-B clears fetal cells quickly, before they can sensitize her to D.

test.q: Severe fetal anemia with generalized fluid accumulation is called:
test.explain: Hydrops fetalis comes from high-output heart failure caused by severe anemia.

test.q: Which event can cause fetomaternal hemorrhage and calls for extra Rh immune globulin?
test.explain: Trauma, amniocentesis, miscarriage and similar events can move fetal cells into maternal blood.

test.q: Where are the Rh genes RHD and RHCE located?
test.explain: RHD and RHCE sit next to each other on chromosome 1. ABO is on chromosome 9.

test.q: What product is given to Rh-negative mothers to prevent anti-D sensitization?
test.explain: Rh immune globulin (passive anti-D) prevents the mother from making her own anti-D.

test.q: Making antibodies against another person's blood group antigens is called ___.
test.explain: Alloimmunization occurs after exposure to foreign red cell antigens through transfusion or pregnancy.

test.q: Fetal anemia is monitored with Doppler of the middle cerebral ___.
test.explain: MCA peak systolic velocity rises in fetal anemia because the blood is less viscous.

kidTest.q: What does Rh positive mean?
choices: Your red cells have the D tag
Your blood has no red cells
kidTest.explain: Rh positive means the red cells wear the D name tag.

kidTest.q: When does a baby's blood usually get into the mom's blood?
kidTest.explain: Most mixing happens at birth.

kidTest.q: What can happen to a later baby if mom has anti-D defenders?
kidTest.explain: The defenders cross over and attack the baby's red cells, which can make the baby sick and yellow.

kidTest.q: How do doctors protect the mom's future babies?
kidTest.explain: A special shot stops the mom's body from learning to fight D.

kidTest.q: The defenders mom's body makes are called a _ _ _ b _ _ _ _ s.
kidTest.explain: Antibodies are the body's defenders against things that look strange. In HDFN, mom's anti-D antibodies can cross the placenta and attack the baby's Rh-positive red blood cells.

advancedTest.q: Why does anti-D cause mainly splenic, extravascular hemolysis rather than complement-mediated lysis?
choices: Anti-D is mostly IgM, which is a poor activator of complement
Fetal red cells lack complement receptors on their surface
D antigen is located inside the red cell cytoskeleton
D sites are sparse and too widely spaced for C1q bridging
advancedTest.explain: C1q needs closely spaced IgG molecules. Sparse D sites prevent this, so FcγR-bearing splenic macrophages clear the coated cells.

advancedTest.q: A D-positive pregnant patient with partial D category DVI makes anti-D. The best explanation is:
choices: Passive anti-D from prophylaxis was misidentified
RHCE silencing triggers loss of self-tolerance
Weak D lowers total antigen density below threshold
Missing D epitopes are recognized as foreign
advancedTest.explain: Partial D cells lack some D epitopes, so the carrier can make alloanti-D against the epitopes she lacks.

advancedTest.q: Why is anti-Kell managed differently from anti-D in alloimmunized pregnancies?
choices: Anti-Kell suppresses fetal erythropoiesis, so anemia occurs at low titers
Anti-Kell is fully prevented by routine Rh immune globulin
Kell antigens first appear after birth on neonatal red cells
Anti-Kell is IgM and does not cross the placenta
advancedTest.explain: Kell is expressed on erythroid progenitors, so anti-Kell suppresses red cell production as well as destroying cells. Titers underestimate the risk.

advancedTest.q: What is the rationale for FcRn blockade (nipocalimab) in severe HDFN?
choices: It increases fetal D expression to dilute anti-D
It lowers maternal IgG and reduces placental IgG transfer
It stimulates fetal complement to clear coated cells
It neutralizes bilirubin before it reaches the brain
advancedTest.explain: FcRn both recycles IgG, extending its half-life, and transports it across the placenta. Blocking it lowers maternal IgG and placental transfer.

lessons.title: Minor Blood Groups: Kell, Duffy, Kidd & Alloimmunization

levels.kid:
You already know about blood types like A, B and O. But red blood cells wear many more tiny name tags on their outside. Scientists have found hundreds of them! Some have funny names, like **Kell**, **Duffy** and **Kidd**. They are named after the families where they were first found.

Most of the time these little tags don't matter. But if someone gets blood with a tag their body has never seen, the body may learn to fight it. That learning is called **alloimmunization**. Next time, the body remembers and may attack those blood cells.

That is why people who get lots of blood, like kids with sickle cell disease, get blood that matches extra carefully. It is like matching puzzle pieces so everything fits.
levels.hs:
Besides ABO and Rh, red blood cells carry many other **antigens**, which are molecules the immune system can recognize. The International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) recognizes over 40 blood group systems with more than 350 antigens. The clinically important "minor" ones include **Kell**, **Duffy**, **Kidd** and **MNS**.

Unlike anti-A and anti-B, which form naturally in early childhood, antibodies to minor antigens usually appear only after exposure to foreign red cells. That can happen through a transfusion or a pregnancy. This process is called **alloimmunization** ("allo" means "other," as in from another person of the same species).

Why it matters:
- A person with an antibody can destroy transfused red cells that carry the matching antigen. This is a **hemolytic transfusion reaction**.
- A pregnant person with an antibody can pass it to the fetus and damage the baby's red cells.

A real example: the **Kell** antigen K is very **immunogenic**, meaning it easily triggers antibodies. Anti-K in pregnancy can cause severe fetal anemia, because it also attacks the cells that make red cells.

People who receive many transfusions, such as those with sickle cell disease, are at highest risk. Blood banks protect them by giving blood that is antigen-matched for Rh and Kell, and sometimes for more antigens.
levels.college:
Minor blood group antigens are encoded by genes outside ABO and RHD. Most are inherited as codominant alleles, and most clinically significant antibodies against them are **IgG**. These antibodies react best at 37 °C and are detected with the antiglobulin test.

**Kell (KEL)**
- Antigens K (Kell) and k (Cellano). About 9% of white people are K-positive; most people are kk.
- K is the most immunogenic antigen after D.
- The Kell glycoprotein is expressed early on erythroid progenitors. Anti-K therefore suppresses red cell production in the fetus, not just hemolysis. Fetal anemia can be severe even with low maternal antibody titers.

**Duffy (FY)**
- Antigens Fya and Fyb on **ACKR1**, a chemokine receptor.
- ACKR1 is the receptor *Plasmodium vivax* uses to invade red cells.
- The Fy(a−b−) phenotype is common in people of West African ancestry. It comes from a GATA-1 promoter mutation that silences expression only in erythroid cells, and it confers resistance to vivax malaria.

**Kidd (JK)**
- Antigens Jka and Jkb on the **urea transporter** UT-B (SLC14A1).
- Kidd antibodies are notorious because they fall below detectable levels over time. On re-exposure they rebound, causing **delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions** about 3 to 14 days later.

**MNS** antigens sit on glycophorins A and B. Anti-M and anti-N are often naturally occurring IgM antibodies of little clinical significance. Anti-S, anti-s and anti-U are IgG antibodies that can cause hemolysis.

**Alloimmunization** affects roughly 2 to 5% of transfused patients overall. In sickle cell disease, historical rates run around 20 to 40%. This is partly because of antigen differences between donors and recipients from different ancestral populations.
levels.phd:
Alloimmunization requires a foreign antigen, enough exposure, and a recipient who can present the antigen's peptides. Minor-antigen polymorphisms are often single amino acid changes. K versus k is a Thr193Met substitution in the Kell glycoprotein, and Fya versus Fyb is Gly42Asp in ACKR1. So responsiveness depends on whether a recipient's HLA class II molecules can present the variant peptide to CD4 T cells. HLA-DRB1 associations have been described for anti-K and anti-Fya. Inflammation at the time of transfusion also modulates risk. In mouse models using the HOD and KEL antigens (Hendrickson, Zimring and colleagues), viral-like inflammation from poly(I:C) boosts alloimmunization. Sickle cell disease patients transfused during acute chest syndrome or vaso-occlusive crises also appear more likely to form new antibodies.

Structural biology explains several clinical behaviors:
- **Kell** is a zinc endopeptidase that cleaves big endothelin-3. It is linked by a disulfide bond to the XK protein. Absence of XK causes **McLeod syndrome**: weak Kell antigens, acanthocytes, and late-onset neuroacanthocytosis with chorea and cardiomyopathy. Because Kell appears on early erythroid progenitors, anti-K suppresses fetal erythropoiesis. As a result, reticulocyte counts and amniotic bilirubin underestimate how anemic the fetus is.
- **Duffy**: the erythroid-silent FY*B^ES allele (c.-67T>C) disrupts a GATA-1 binding site. The antigen still appears on endothelium, so Fy(a−b−) people rarely make anti-Fy3. Duffy-null status also lowers baseline neutrophil counts ("Duffy-null associated neutrophil count"). This was formerly mislabeled benign ethnic neutropenia.
- **Kidd**: people who are Jk(a−b−) (common in Polynesian populations, often from a JK*null splice variant) lack UT-B. They have a mild urine-concentrating defect, and their red cells resist lysis in 2 M urea, which offers a screening trick. Kidd antibodies often bind complement and show **dosage**: they react more strongly with homozygous Jk(a+b−) cells than with heterozygous cells.

The evanescence of anti-Jka reflects short-lived plasma cell responses. Persistent memory B cells then drive a fast anamnestic rebound. Antibody records shared across hospitals, rather than the current screen alone, are what prevent delayed hemolysis.
levels.expert:
Clinical practice now centers on preventing antibodies, not just detecting them.

**Prophylactic matching.** The 2020 ASH guidelines for sickle cell disease recommend Rh (C, E or C/c, E/e) and K antigen matching. Extended matching (Jk, Fy, S) is suggested for patients who are already alloimmunized. Even so, RH genetic diversity defeats serologic matching. Variant RHD and RHCE alleles (for example, partial C carried by RHCE*ce48C, or RHD*DIIIa) mean an apparent match can still immunize. Programs such as Bloodworks Northwest and the NHS's sickle genotyping project use RH genotyping of patients and donors. Increasing donations from donors of matching ancestry matters as much as the technology.

**Hyperhemolysis.** Some patients destroy both donor and their own red cells after transfusion, so hemoglobin falls below the pre-transfusion level. Often no new antibody is found, which suggests macrophage activation rather than a classic antibody reaction. Management means avoiding further transfusion when possible. IVIG, steroids, and in refractory cases eculizumab or tocilizumab have been reported.

**Pregnancy.** Kell-sensitized pregnancies need a lower critical titer (often 8) than anti-D pregnancies. Monitoring uses middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity Doppler, not amniotic bilirubin. Fetal genotyping from cell-free DNA in maternal plasma (for K, RhC, RhE) can spare antigen-negative fetuses from monitoring. Nipocalimab, an FcRn blocker that limits placental IgG transfer, showed benefit in early-onset HDFN in the phase 2 UNITY trial.

**Lab pitfalls.**
- **Daratumumab** (anti-CD38) makes every panel cell react. Treating cells with DTT fixes this but destroys Kell antigens, so K-negative units are issued empirically.
- Recent transfusion invalidates serologic phenotyping. Molecular typing works around this.
- Antibodies to high-prevalence antigens (anti-Kpb, anti-Jk3, anti-Fy3, anti-U) may require rare-donor registries or frozen units.

**Open questions** remain. Why do only about a third of chronically transfused patients ever alloimmunize (the "responder" phenotype)? Can genotype-matched or stem-cell-derived red cells make universal extended matching practical?

keyPoints: Beyond ABO/Rh, over 40 blood group systems exist; Kell, Duffy, Kidd and MNS matter most clinically
Alloimmunization: antibodies form after exposure to foreign red cells via transfusion or pregnancy
Kell (K) is highly immunogenic; anti-K suppresses fetal red cell production
Duffy (ACKR1) is the P. vivax receptor; the Fy(a−b−) phenotype protects against vivax malaria
Kidd antibodies fade and rebound, causing delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions
Sickle cell patients get Rh and K matched blood to prevent alloimmunization

test.q: What does alloimmunization mean in transfusion medicine?
choices: Gradually losing ABO antibodies with advancing age
Forming antibodies against the person's own red cells
Receiving ready-made antibodies through a vaccine shot
Making antibodies to another person's red cells
test.explain: Allo means 'other.' Alloantibodies form after exposure to foreign red cells, such as through transfusion or pregnancy. Antibodies against one's own cells would be autoantibodies.

test.q: After the D antigen, which red cell antigen is the most immunogenic?
test.explain: The Kell antigen K is the most immunogenic antigen after D.

test.q: Why can anti-K cause severe fetal anemia even when titers are low?
choices: It crosses the placenta as IgM antibody
It suppresses early red cell progenitors
It blocks iron uptake in the fetal gut
test.explain: Kell is expressed on early erythroid progenitors, so anti-K suppresses red cell production as well as causing hemolysis.

test.q: The Duffy glycoprotein serves as the red cell entry receptor for:
test.explain: P. vivax uses Duffy (ACKR1) to invade red cells, so Fy(a−b−) people resist vivax malaria.

test.q: Kidd antibodies are notorious for causing:
test.explain: Kidd antibodies fall below detection, then rebound on re-exposure, causing hemolysis days later.

test.q: The Kidd antigens are carried on which protein?
test.explain: Jka and Jkb sit on the urea transporter UT-B. Duffy is the chemokine receptor and Kell is the endopeptidase.

test.q: Unlike anti-A and anti-B, most antibodies to Kell, Duffy and Kidd antigens:
choices: Are IgM and react best when cold
test.explain: Clinically significant minor-antigen antibodies are usually IgG and arise after transfusion or pregnancy.

test.q: Which patient group has the highest alloimmunization rates?
test.explain: Chronic transfusion plus antigen differences between donors and recipients gave historical rates around 20 to 40% in sickle cell disease.

test.q: Anti-M and anti-N antibodies are usually:
test.explain: Anti-M and anti-N are often naturally occurring IgM antibodies. Anti-S, anti-s and anti-U are the MNS antibodies of concern.

test.q: The Fy(a−b−) phenotype results from a promoter mutation in a binding site for the transcription factor ___.
test.explain: Disrupting the GATA-1 site silences Duffy only in erythroid cells.

test.q: Which X-linked syndrome with acanthocytes and weak Kell antigens results from absent XK protein?
test.explain: McLeod syndrome causes weak Kell expression, acanthocytosis and later neurologic and cardiac problems.

test.q: A molecule on red cells that the immune system can recognize is called an ___.
test.explain: Blood group antigens are recognized by antibodies and can trigger alloimmunization.

kidTest.q: What are Kell, Duffy and Kidd?
choices: Blood group tags on red cells
kidTest.explain: They are blood group tags, called antigens, on red cells.

kidTest.q: Where did these blood groups get their names?
choices: From the cities with big hospitals
From families where they were found
From the colors of the blood
kidTest.explain: They were named after the families where they were first discovered.

kidTest.q: What can happen when the body sees a new blood tag?
choices: It may learn to fight it
kidTest.explain: The body can make antibodies and remember the tag next time.

kidTest.q: Who gets blood matched extra carefully?
choices: People who get lots of blood
kidTest.explain: People like kids with sickle cell disease get many transfusions, so careful matching protects them.

kidTest.q: The minor blood group that shares its name with young children is K _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Kidd is one of the important minor blood groups.

advancedTest.q: In a Kell-sensitized pregnancy, why is MCA Doppler preferred over amniotic bilirubin?
choices: Kell antigens are absent in the fetus until the third trimester
Anti-K is IgM, so amniotic bilirubin stays falsely high throughout pregnancy
Doppler directly measures the maternal antibody titer in fetal blood
Anti-K suppresses red cell production, so hemolysis markers underestimate anemia
advancedTest.explain: Kell is expressed on early progenitors. Anemia comes from suppressed production more than from hemolysis, so bilirubin underestimates severity.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a historical anti-Jka now has a negative screen. What explains the risk of transfusing Jka+ blood?
choices: Kidd antigens grow stronger on stored donor red cells over time
Anti-Jka converts to an autoantibody during dormancy
Memory B cells drive an anamnestic rebound after re-exposure
Negative screens indicate permanent tolerance to Jka
advancedTest.explain: Kidd antibodies fall below detection but rebound quickly, which is why shared antibody records matter more than the current screen.

advancedTest.q: For a patient on daratumumab, panel cells are treated with DTT. Why are K-negative units then issued?
choices: CD38 is physically linked to the Kell protein
DTT converts K-positive cells into k cells
DTT destroys Kell antigens, hiding any anti-K
advancedTest.explain: DTT breaks the disulfide bonds that Kell structure depends on, so anti-K can't be excluded. K-negative blood avoids that risk.

advancedTest.q: Why do Fy(a−b−) individuals with the GATA-1 promoter mutation rarely make anti-Fy3?
choices: Duffy is still expressed on their endothelium, inducing tolerance
Fy3 is carried on the Kidd urea transporter instead
Their red cells carry Fya at very low density
Their HLA molecules are unable to present Duffy peptides
advancedTest.explain: The mutation silences Duffy only in erythroid cells. Endothelial expression means the immune system sees the protein as self.

lessons.title: Type & Screen, Crossmatch & the Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test

levels.kid:
Before someone gets blood from a donor, the hospital lab plays a careful matching game.

First, they check the patient's **blood type**, like reading a name tag on the red cells. Next, they look in the patient's blood for tiny guards called **antibodies**. Some antibodies would attack the wrong donor cells.

Then comes a practice test. The lab mixes a little of the patient's blood liquid with the donor's red cells in a tube. If the cells clump together like sticky cereal, it is a bad match. If they stay smooth, it is a good match.

Some antibodies are too small to make clumps on their own. So the lab adds a special helper called **Coombs reagent**. It acts like a bridge that links them, so hidden problems show up.
levels.hs:
Giving the wrong blood can make the patient's immune system destroy the donor's red cells. This is called a **hemolytic transfusion reaction**. Labs prevent it with **pretransfusion testing**.

- **Type**: the lab finds the patient's ABO group and RhD type. It tests the red cells with known antibodies (the **forward type**). It also tests the plasma against known A and B cells (the **reverse type**). The two results must agree.
- **Screen**: the patient's plasma is mixed with two or three reagent red cells. Together these cells carry the important minor antigens, such as Kell, Duffy and Kidd. The screen looks for **unexpected antibodies**, usually made after earlier transfusions or pregnancies.
- **Crossmatch**: the patient's plasma is tested against the actual donor unit.

The key tool is the **antiglobulin test**, also called the **Coombs test**. Coombs reagent is made of antibodies against human antibodies (IgG) and against complement. It links cells that are coated with antibody, so they clump, which is called **agglutination**.

- The **direct antiglobulin test (DAT)** asks whether the patient's own red cells are already coated inside the body.
- The **indirect antiglobulin test (IAT)** asks whether the plasma contains antibodies that could coat other red cells in the test tube.

Example: a newborn with jaundice whose DAT is positive may have maternal antibodies attached to its red cells.
levels.college:
**Agglutination basics.** IgM antibodies (anti-A, anti-B) are large pentamers. They bridge red cells directly, so they agglutinate at room temperature in saline. IgG antibodies, such as anti-D, anti-K, anti-Fya and anti-Jka, are small. Red cells normally repel each other because of negative surface charge (zeta potential), and IgG cannot span that gap. IgG therefore coats cells without clumping them. **Anti-human globulin (AHG)**, introduced by Coombs, Mourant and Race in 1945, cross-links the IgG-coated cells.

**IAT steps:**
- Incubate plasma with reagent or donor cells at 37°C, often with an enhancement medium such as LISS or PEG.
- Wash the cells to remove unbound globulin. Otherwise free IgG would neutralize the AHG and cause a false negative.
- Add AHG and look for agglutination.
- Add **check cells** (IgG-coated cells) to any negative tube. They should agglutinate, which proves the AHG was still active.

**DAT.** The patient's cells are washed and tested with polyspecific AHG, then with monospecific anti-IgG and anti-C3d. A positive DAT is seen in warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (usually IgG with or without C3), cold agglutinin disease (C3 only), drug-induced hemolysis, HDFN and delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions.

**Type and screen vs crossmatch.**
- A **type and screen** is enough for procedures with a low chance of needing blood.
- If the screen is negative, an **immediate-spin crossmatch** (a few minutes at room temperature) confirms ABO compatibility. An **electronic crossmatch** by computer is another option when validated rules are met: two concordant ABO types and a negative screen.
- If the screen is positive, the lab **identifies the antibody** with a cell panel. It then gives antigen-negative units and performs a full **AHG crossmatch**.

**Emergencies.** Uncrossmatched group O red cells can be released before testing is finished.
levels.phd:
**Why the antiglobulin phase is needed.** A red cell carries a negative charge mainly from sialic acid on glycophorins, which creates a zeta potential. The IgG Fab arms span only about 12 nm, too short to bridge two cells. IgM spans about 30 nm, enough to bridge cells at saline separation. Enhancement methods work in different ways:
- **LISS** lowers ionic strength, which speeds antibody uptake.
- **PEG** excludes water and concentrates the antibody.
- **Enzymes** (ficin, papain) cleave sialoglycoproteins. This strengthens Rh and Kidd reactions but destroys M, N, S, Fya and Fyb. The enzyme effect is a classic clue in antibody identification.

**Platforms.** Tube testing has largely given way to **column agglutination** (gel or glass bead) and **solid-phase red cell adherence**. In gel cards, agglutinates are trapped and graded 0 to 4+, and the AHG is built into the gel, so no washing is needed. Solid-phase tests are very sensitive. They detect more clinically insignificant antibodies, which trades specificity for sensitivity.

**Panel interpretation.** A typical panel has about 11 group O cells with known phenotypes. The analyst **rules out** antigens on nonreactive cells, preferably using homozygous cells for antigens that show **dosage** (Kidd, Duffy, MNS, and Rh C/c/E/e). The usual rule of three (three positive and three negative cells) gives p≈0.05 for confirming a specificity. An **autocontrol** or DAT separates autoantibody from alloantibody.

**Interferences.**
- **Daratumumab** (anti-CD38) binds CD38 on reagent cells and causes panreactivity in the IAT. Treating cells with DTT removes CD38 but also destroys Kell antigens, so K-negative units are given.
- Strong warm autoantibodies mask alloantibodies. **Adsorption** (autologous or allogeneic) can uncover them.
- Rouleaux (stacked red cells) and cold autoantibodies can produce false positives at immediate spin.

**DAT nuance.** A positive DAT is found in roughly 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 14,000 healthy donors and in up to about 15% of hospitalized patients. Positivity alone is not proof of hemolysis; it must be interpreted alongside laboratory hemolysis markers. **Eluates** (stripping antibody from the cells with acid or heat) identify the specificity of the bound antibody.
levels.expert:
**Clinical judgement, not just bench steps.**

- **Specimen identity is the dominant risk.** Most ABO-incompatible transfusions come from patient or sample misidentification, called **wrong blood in tube (WBIT)**, not from failures of serologic tests. That is why many institutions require a second, separately drawn ABO sample before issuing non-O red cells or allowing the electronic crossmatch. Bedside two-person or barcode verification adds another layer.
- **Sample validity windows.** If a patient was transfused or pregnant within the last 3 months, the screen sample is typically valid for only 3 days. New alloantibodies can appear within days of exposure.
- **Evanescent antibodies.** Kidd antibodies often fall below detection, leaving a negative screen. On re-exposure they cause **delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions** (DHTR) 3 to 14 days later. Antibody history files, including shared regional databases, therefore take precedence over a negative current screen.
- **Sickle cell disease.** Patients are prophylactically matched for Rh (C, E, often D variants) and K. Many are genotyped, because RHD/RHCE variants are common in people of African ancestry. DHTR here can cause **hyperhemolysis**, in which the patient's own red cells are also destroyed. In that setting the DAT may be negative, which is a well-known pitfall.
- **Molecular immunohematology.** SNP-based red cell genotyping (for example, the FDA-cleared ID CORE XT) predicts phenotype in recently transfused patients and in patients on daratumumab, where serology is unreliable. Recombinant soluble CD38 to neutralize anti-CD38 interference is being studied.
- **Massive bleeding.** Emergency-release O-negative units are reserved for females of childbearing potential, because anti-D carries a risk of HDFN in future pregnancies. Many centres give O-positive units to males. Antibody screens on pretransfusion samples should still be completed retrospectively.
- **Reading a positive DAT.** In suspected DHTR, a mixed-field DAT with an eluate showing a new alloantibody is diagnostic. A positive DAT with a nonreactive eluate in a patient on ceftriaxone points to drug-dependent antibodies.

**Open questions:** whether genotype-matched supply can be scaled, how to make electronic crossmatching more widespread, and how to reduce WBIT with point-of-care identification.

keyPoints: Type = ABO/RhD by forward and reverse typing; screen = search for unexpected antibodies
IgM antibodies agglutinate directly; IgG needs anti-human globulin (Coombs reagent)
DAT detects antibody/complement already on cells in the body; IAT detects antibody in plasma in vitro
Negative screen allows immediate-spin or electronic crossmatch; positive screen needs antibody ID and AHG crossmatch
Washing and check cells prevent false-negative antiglobulin tests
Wrong blood in tube, evanescent Kidd antibodies and daratumumab are major pitfalls

test.q: What does the antibody screen look for?
test.explain: The screen mixes plasma with reagent cells to detect unexpected alloantibodies such as anti-K or anti-Jka.

test.q: Why is Coombs reagent needed to detect most IgG antibodies?
choices: IgG is too small to bridge red cells
IgG is absent from adult plasma
IgG destroys the red cells at once
IgG binds mainly at cold temperatures
test.explain: IgG coats cells but cannot span the gap from red cell surface charge; the antiglobulin cross-links the coated cells.

test.q: The direct antiglobulin test (DAT) detects:
choices: ABO antigens present on donor red cells
Iron stores held inside the red cells
Antibodies circulating free in the plasma
Antibody or complement on cells in vivo
test.explain: The DAT tests the patient's own washed red cells for coating that occurred in the body; the IAT tests plasma.

test.q: Reverse typing tests the patient's:
choices: Red cells with anti-A and anti-B
Plasma with known A and B cells
test.explain: Reverse typing looks for anti-A and anti-B in plasma; forward typing tests the cells.

test.q: A patient has a negative antibody screen and concordant ABO types. Which crossmatch is usually enough?
test.explain: With a negative screen, only ABO compatibility needs confirming, by immediate spin or computer.

test.q: Why are cells washed before the antiglobulin reagent is added?
choices: To remove complement from the cells
To strip IgM from the surface
To lower the cells' surface charge
To stop free IgG neutralizing the reagent
test.explain: Unbound plasma IgG would consume the anti-IgG and cause a false negative.

test.q: Which pattern fits cold agglutinin disease?
test.explain: Cold IgM fixes complement then detaches, leaving C3d on cells; warm AIHA is typically IgG.

test.q: In a massive bleed before testing, what is usually released?
test.explain: Group O red cells lack A and B antigens, so they can be given before typing is complete.

test.q: What is the main cause of ABO-incompatible transfusions?
choices: Weak or faulty anti-A typing reagents
test.explain: Wrong blood in tube and bedside identity errors dominate; serologic test failure is rare.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for the test that detects plasma antibodies by incubating them with red cells in vitro?
test.explain: The indirect antiglobulin test underlies the screen and the AHG crossmatch.

test.q: Clumping of red cells by antibody is called ___.
test.explain: Agglutination is the visible endpoint of blood bank tests.

test.q: IgG-coated ___ cells are added to negative tubes to prove the antiglobulin reagent worked.
test.explain: Check cells should agglutinate; if they don't, the negative result is invalid.

kidTest.q: What does it mean if cells clump in the test tube?
kidTest.explain: Clumping means antibodies are attacking the cells.

kidTest.q: What are the tiny guards the lab looks for in blood?
kidTest.explain: Antibodies can attack the wrong donor cells.

kidTest.q: What does Coombs reagent do?
choices: Links cells so hidden problems show
kidTest.explain: It acts like a bridge so small antibodies make clumps.

kidTest.q: What does the lab check first?
kidTest.explain: Blood type is like a name tag on the red cells.

kidTest.q: Bad matches make red cells form c _ _ _ _ s.
kidTest.explain: Clumps show the donor blood would be attacked.

advancedTest.q: In a myeloma patient, a panel reacts with all cells and the autocontrol at immediate spin. The reactions disperse with saline replacement and are absent at the washed AHG phase. The DAT is negative. The likeliest cause is:
choices: An evanescent anti-Jka below detection limits
A warm autoantibody coating the patient's own cells
Interference from anti-CD38 therapy such as daratumumab
advancedTest.explain: Paraprotein causes rouleaux. This gives pseudo-agglutination of all cells, including the autocontrol, in unwashed phases such as immediate spin, and saline replacement disperses it. Washing removes the plasma, so the AHG phase and the DAT are negative. Daratumumab causes panreactivity mainly at the AHG phase, and DTT treatment of reagent cells abolishes it. A warm autoantibody would usually give a positive DAT and AHG-phase reactivity.

advancedTest.q: A reaction disappears when the panel cells are treated with ficin. Which specificity does this favour?
advancedTest.explain: Enzymes destroy Duffy and MNS antigens, but they enhance Rh and Kidd reactions.

advancedTest.q: Ten days after transfusion, the hemoglobin falls and a new mixed-field DAT appears, while the prior screen was negative. The best explanation is:
choices: An anamnestic response from an evanescent alloantibody
Acute ABO incompatibility from a typing error
A false-positive DAT caused by the storage lesion
Cold agglutinin disease triggered by the stored blood
advancedTest.explain: Kidd and similar antibodies fall below detection, then rebound on re-exposure. This causes a delayed hemolytic reaction that coats only the donor cells, giving a mixed-field DAT.

advancedTest.q: Why should anti-Jka be ruled out using a homozygous Jk(a+b−) cell?
choices: Heterozygous cells carry no Jka antigen on their surface
Homozygous cells resist enzyme destruction better
Kidd antigens appear mainly on reagent group O cells
Dosage lets weak antibodies miss heterozygous cells
advancedTest.explain: Kidd antigens show dosage. Heterozygous cells carry less antigen, so a weak antibody can give a falsely negative reaction.

lessons.title: Blood Donation, Component Processing & the Storage Lesion

levels.kid:
When a grown-up gives blood, a nurse puts a tiny tube in their arm. A bag slowly fills up with blood. It takes about ten minutes, and then the donor gets a snack!

But the blood does not stay all mixed together. At the blood bank, the bag goes into a machine that spins it super fast, like a merry-go-round. The heavy red cells sink to the bottom. The yellow liquid, called **plasma**, floats on top. Tiny pieces called **platelets** end up in the middle.

Now one gift can help several sick people. Red cells go in the fridge. Plasma goes in the freezer. Platelets stay at room temperature on a gentle rocker.

Blood is a bit like bread. It is best fresh, and it slowly changes while it is stored.
levels.hs:
**Blood donation** collects blood from healthy volunteers. Before donating, people answer health questions and get a quick check of hemoglobin and blood pressure. This protects the donor and the patient. A standard whole-blood donation is about 450-500 mL, roughly a tenth of an adult's blood volume. The body rebuilds the plasma within a day or two and the red cells over several weeks.

The bag contains an **anticoagulant-preservative** solution. Citrate stops clotting by binding calcium. Glucose (dextrose) feeds the red cells. The bag is then **centrifuged** (spun hard) and split into **components**:
- **Red blood cells (RBCs)**: refrigerated at 1-6 °C. They last up to about 42 days in an additive solution.
- **Plasma**: frozen within hours. It can be stored for a year or more and holds the clotting factors.
- **Platelets**: kept at 20-24 °C with gentle shaking. They expire after just 5-7 days.
- **Cryoprecipitate**: made by thawing frozen plasma slowly in the cold. It is rich in fibrinogen.

Each donated unit is tested for its blood group and screened for infections such as HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis.

Stored red cells slowly change over time. Doctors call this the **storage lesion**. The cells use up energy, become stiffer, and leak potassium. Think of milk in the fridge: it is safe until its date, but it is not quite the same as fresh.
levels.college:
**Collection.** Whole blood is drawn into a bag containing **CPD** (citrate-phosphate-dextrose) or a similar solution:
- **Citrate** chelates Ca²⁺, which blocks the calcium-dependent steps of coagulation.
- **Phosphate** buffers pH.
- **Dextrose** fuels red cell glycolysis.

**Apheresis** is the other way to collect. A machine draws blood, keeps one component (platelets, plasma, or two red cell units) and returns the rest to the donor.

**Processing.**
- A soft spin separates platelet-rich plasma; a hard spin then pellets the platelets. Alternatively, the **buffy-coat** method pools platelets from several donors.
- Red cells are resuspended in an **additive solution** such as SAGM (saline, adenine, glucose, mannitol) or AS-1/AS-3. This extends shelf life to 42 days.
- Plasma frozen within 8 hours becomes **fresh frozen plasma (FFP)**, which preserves the labile factors V and VIII.
- **Cryoprecipitate** is the cold-insoluble fraction of FFP. It is rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, factor XIII and fibronectin.

**Modifications.**
- **Leukoreduction** filters out white cells. This reduces febrile reactions, HLA alloimmunization and CMV transmission.
- **Irradiation** inactivates donor lymphocytes, which prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GVHD).
- **Washing** removes plasma proteins.

**Storage temperatures.** Platelets are stored warm because cold triggers their clearance, but warm storage raises the risk of bacterial contamination.

**The storage lesion** describes the changes in refrigerated RBCs over time:
- **2,3-BPG** falls to near zero within about 2 weeks. This raises oxygen affinity (left shift). Levels recover within hours to days after transfusion.
- **ATP** declines, and the cells become stiffer and more spherical.
- The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase slows in the cold, so **extracellular K⁺** rises in the bag.
- Hemolysis increases, and microvesicles accumulate.
- Lactate builds up and pH falls.

Regulators require at least 75% of transfused cells to survive 24 hours after transfusion.
levels.phd:
**Metabolic basis.** Refrigeration slows red cell glycolysis but does not stop it. Acidification inhibits **bisphosphoglycerate mutase** and favors 2,3-BPG phosphatase activity, so 2,3-BPG is depleted early. In vivo regeneration takes roughly 24-72 hours. Oxidative stress, including impaired glutathione and NADPH handling, oxidizes band 3 and spectrin. This causes clustering of band 3 and exposure of **phosphatidylserine**, which marks cells for macrophage removal. **Vesiculation** sheds membrane and lowers the surface-to-volume ratio, so cells lose deformability. Some cells progress from echinocytes to spheroechinocytes, which are cleared irreversibly within hours of transfusion.

**Nitric oxide and iron.** Free hemoglobin and microvesicles scavenge **nitric oxide** about 1000-fold faster than intact cells, which is proposed to impair vasodilation. Rapid clearance of damaged cells delivers a bolus of iron to macrophages. In Hod's human studies, older units produced circulating non-transferrin-bound iron, a plausible link to inflammation and bacterial growth.

**Genetic modifiers.** Donors differ in how well their cells store. The REDS-III RBC-Omics program linked storage hemolysis to donor sex, G6PD status, and variants such as SEC14L4 and ATP11C (a phosphatidylserine flippase).

**The controversy.** Observational data, notably Koch's 2008 cardiac surgery study, associated older blood with higher mortality. Randomized trials did not confirm this:
- **ABLE** and **RECESS** (2015), and **INFORM** (2016, about 31,000 patients) found no benefit of fresher units.
- **TRANSFUSE** (2017) in ICU patients was also neutral.

The current reading is that average outcomes within the licensed 42-day window are equivalent. Subgroups, extreme storage ages, and massive transfusion remain uncertain.

**Platelet storage lesion.** At 22 °C, platelets show progressive activation, glycolytic lactate production, and loss of the swirling sign (discoid shape). Cold exposure clusters GPIbα. Desialylation then triggers hepatic Ashwell-Morell receptor clearance, so cold platelets circulate briefly. They are, however, hemostatically more reactive.
levels.expert:
**Pathogen safety.** Residual transfusion-transmitted infection risk now centers on bacteria in platelets. Sepsis from contaminated platelets historically occurred in roughly 1 in a few thousand to 10,000 units. FDA's 2019-revised guidance (finalized 2020) offers two main strategies:
- **Large-volume delayed sampling** culture, or secondary testing, which can extend shelf life to 7 days.
- **Pathogen reduction**, such as amotosalen plus UVA (INTERCEPT). This crosslinks nucleic acids and inactivates bacteria, viruses, parasites and lymphocytes, and can substitute for irradiation. The trade-off is modestly lower count increments.

Whole-blood pathogen reduction (riboflavin-UV, amustaline) is in trials.

**Cold-stored platelets and whole blood.** Interest is reviving:
- FDA allows 2-6 °C platelets for bleeding patients when conventional units are unavailable, with storage up to 14 days.
- **Low-titer group O whole blood** is increasingly used in trauma and prehospital care.
- The CHIPS trial in cardiac surgery is evaluating cold-stored platelets.

**Storage-lesion pitfalls at the bedside.**
- **Hyperkalemia** is a real risk in neonates, in large or rapid transfusions, and when blood runs through central lines close to the heart. Fresher or washed units mitigate it.
- **Citrate toxicity** (ionized hypocalcemia) occurs in massive transfusion or liver failure, where citrate cannot be metabolized quickly. Monitor ionized calcium.
- **Irradiation** accelerates potassium leak and shortens RBC expiry.
- Mixing up these unit modifications harms the patients who need them: irradiated units for TA-GVHD risk, CMV-safe units for vulnerable recipients.

**Donor-side issues.** Frequent donors and teenagers risk **iron deficiency**. The REDS-II RISE study and the HEIRS findings drove ferritin testing, iron supplementation advice, and longer donation intervals in some programs. Vasovagal reactions are commonest in young first-time donors. Donor policies are shifting: the FDA's 2023 individual risk-based questions replaced time-based deferrals for men who have sex with men.

**Frontiers.**
- **Hypoxic (anaerobic) storage** limits oxidative damage; one system has received FDA clearance.
- **Rejuvenation solutions** (pyruvate, inosine, phosphate, adenine) restore 2,3-BPG.
- Lab-grown red cells are under study; the RESTORE trial is examining whether cultured cells survive longer.
- **Freeze-dried plasma** is available for military use.

Open question: can quality metrics for each unit (hemolysis, metabolomics) identify bad storers before issue?

keyPoints: Whole blood is collected into citrate-based anticoagulant and spun into components
RBCs at 1-6 °C up to 42 days, plasma frozen, platelets at 20-24 °C for 5-7 days
Cryoprecipitate is the cold-insoluble part of plasma, rich in fibrinogen
Leukoreduction, irradiation and washing modify components for specific risks
Storage lesion: falling 2,3-BPG and ATP, rising potassium, stiffer cells, hemolysis
Large trials (ABLE, RECESS, INFORM) found no benefit of fresher red cells

test.q: How does citrate in a collection bag prevent clotting?
test.explain: Citrate chelates Ca²⁺, which the clotting cascade needs. Antithrombin activation is how heparin works, not citrate.

test.q: At what temperature are platelets stored?
test.explain: Platelets are kept at room temperature with agitation because cold triggers their rapid clearance.

test.q: Which component is especially rich in fibrinogen?
test.explain: Cryoprecipitate is the cold-insoluble fraction of plasma and contains fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF and factor XIII.

test.q: What happens to 2,3-BPG in stored red cells?
choices: It is converted directly into lactate
It stays roughly constant in storage
It falls to near zero within 2 weeks
It rises steadily over several weeks
test.explain: 2,3-BPG is depleted early in storage, which increases hemoglobin's oxygen affinity until it regenerates after transfusion.

test.q: Why does potassium rise in the plasma of a stored red cell unit?
choices: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump slows in the cold
test.explain: Cold storage and falling ATP slow the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, so potassium leaks out of the cells and accumulates in the bag.

test.q: Irradiating a blood component mainly prevents which complication?
test.explain: Irradiation inactivates donor lymphocytes that could attack the recipient. Febrile reactions are reduced by leukoreduction instead.

test.q: Why do platelets have the shortest shelf life of the major components?
choices: They lose their blood group antigens
test.explain: Room-temperature storage lets contaminating bacteria multiply, which limits platelets to about 5-7 days.

test.q: What did the ABLE, RECESS and INFORM trials conclude?
choices: Older red cells raised infection rates
Storage age mattered for cardiac surgery
Fresher red cells gave no clear benefit
test.explain: These randomized trials found no outcome advantage for fresher units, unlike earlier observational studies.

test.q: Leukoreduction lowers the risk of which of these?
test.explain: Removing white cells reduces febrile reactions, HLA alloimmunization and CMV transmission.

test.q: Collecting a single component by machine and returning the rest to the donor is called ___.
test.explain: Apheresis machines separate blood during donation and keep only the desired component.

test.q: What is the general name for the progressive changes red cells undergo during refrigerated storage?
test.explain: The storage lesion includes lost 2,3-BPG and ATP, potassium leak, stiffer cells, vesiculation and hemolysis.

test.q: Plasma frozen within 8 hours of collection is called ___ frozen plasma (FFP).
test.explain: Fresh frozen plasma preserves the labile clotting factors V and VIII.

kidTest.q: What does the blood bank machine do to the blood?
kidTest.explain: Spinning makes the heavy red cells sink and the plasma float on top.

kidTest.q: Where do red cells go after they are separated?
kidTest.explain: Red cells are kept cold in a fridge.

kidTest.q: What color is plasma?
kidTest.explain: Plasma is the yellow liquid part of blood.

kidTest.q: Why is splitting the blood helpful?
choices: It makes the blood taste better
It makes the bag lighter to carry
kidTest.explain: Each part can go to a different patient who needs it.

kidTest.q: Tiny blood pieces that stay on a gentle rocker are called p _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Platelets are kept at room temperature and gently rocked.

advancedTest.q: A neonate receiving a rapid exchange transfusion is at particular risk from which storage-lesion feature?
choices: High extracellular potassium in the unit
advancedTest.explain: Potassium that leaks into the bag can cause dangerous hyperkalemia with large or rapid volumes in small patients. Low 2,3-BPG gives a left shift, not a right shift.

advancedTest.q: Why did observational studies suggest harm from old blood while RCTs did not?
choices: Sicker patients likely received more, and older, units
The RCTs used frozen rather than refrigerated units
The RCTs excluded units stored past 7 days
advancedTest.explain: Confounding by illness severity and transfusion volume can link older units with worse outcomes without causation.

advancedTest.q: Why do cold-stored platelets circulate briefly yet remain attractive for actively bleeding trauma patients?
choices: Cold storage removes their HLA antigens
Cold storage increases their count after transfusion
They are cleared quickly but are more reactive
advancedTest.explain: GPIbα clustering and desialylation drive rapid hepatic clearance, but cold platelets are hemostatically more active, which matters most for immediate bleeding.

advancedTest.q: Which approach can substitute for irradiation while also addressing bacterial risk in platelets?
advancedTest.explain: Amotosalen-UVA crosslinks nucleic acids, inactivating pathogens and lymphocytes. Culture detects bacteria but does not inactivate lymphocytes.
